query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing an ultrathin, dense alumina layer via atomic layer deposition (ALD) on boride-based components will significantly improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by acting as an effective diffusion barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-coated components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that currently suffer from aggressive molten-aluminum attack.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultrathin (~several nanometers), dense alumina (Al2O3) coating using ALD as a single-step surface modification.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at temperatures between 600–750°C typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating, with prolonged contact times.
generation.structural_mediator: The deposited alumina layer acts as a chemically inert, adherent barrier that suppresses aluminum diffusion and interfacial reactions with the underlying boride layer.
generation.mechanism: The thermodynamically stable alumina reduces interdiffusion and chemical attack at the boride–aluminum interface by providing a physical and chemical barrier, thereby limiting the corrosive interaction between molten aluminum and the boride-based component.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated boride coatings, the ALD alumina–coated components will exhibit substantially reduced weight loss and maintain more intact surface microstructure after prolonged molten-aluminum exposure, indicating improved corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components with standard coatings and without the ALD alumina layer.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness is expected to hold under consistent hot-dip plating conditions (600–750°C, continuous molten aluminum contact); performance beyond these thermal limits or under extreme thermal cycling remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in corrosion resistance (e.g., percentage reduction in weight loss) depend on the specific thickness and quality of the alumina layer and its long-term adhesion under cyclic thermal stresses; these factors require further experimental clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based component samples: one set with the ALD-deposited ultrathin alumina coating and one set without. Expose both sets to molten aluminum at 700°C for a fixed duration. Evaluate corrosion by weight loss measurements and microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM, XRD) post-exposure.
measurements: Phase composition via XRD or XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ALD alumina–coated components do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion (measured by weight loss and microstructural degradation) compared to the uncoated controls under identical molten-aluminum exposure conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys were treated by powder-pack boriding to improve their surface hardness and wear resistance. The variation of boriding layer thickness with time and temperature was studied. Then, the frequency factor D0 and diffusion activation energy Q of element B in HEA are calculated to be 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s and 206.93 kJ/mol, respectively. The diffusion behavior of elements in the boronizing process was investigated and shows that the boride layer forms with the metal atoms diffusing outward and the diffusion layer forms with the B atoms diffusing inward by the Pt-labeling method. In addition, the surface microhardness of CoCrFeNiMn HEA was significantly improved to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa, and the friction coefficient was reduced from 0.86 to 0.48~0.61.Keywords: high entropy alloy, boronizing, growth kinetics, boronizing mechanism, wear resistance

AbstractSurface condition and corrosion resistance are major concerns when metallic materials are going to be utilized for applications. In this study, FeCoNiCr medium-entropy alloy (MEA) is first treated with a nitrogen atmospheric-pressure plasma jet (APPJ) and then coated with octadecyltrichlorosilane (OTS) for the surface modification. The hydrophobicity of the FeCoNiCr MEA was effectively improved by OTS-coating treatment, APPJ treatment, or the combination of both treatments (OTS-coated APPJ-treated), which increased the water contact angle from 54.49° of the bare MEA to 70.56°, 93.94°, and 88.42°, respectively. Potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy tests demonstrate that the APPJ-treated FeCoNiCr MEA exhibits the best anti-corrosion properties. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals that APPJ treatment at 700 °C oxidizes all the alloying elements in the FeCoNiCr MEA, which demonstrates that a short APPJ treatment of two-minute is effective in forming a metal oxide layer on the surface to improve the corrosion resistance of FeCoNiCr MEA. These results provide a convenient and rapid method for improving surface properties of FeCoNiCr MEA.Key

decision.trend: Earlier work on protective alloy surfaces has moved from simply applying standard coatings to using tailored surface treatments that modify the near‐surface microstructure and chemistry. For example, the powder-pack boronizing of a high-entropy alloy (PMC10221107) successfully formed a reinforced, boride-rich surface layer, while plasma and silane treatments (PMC7240591) demonstrated that even a short, controlled surface oxidation can lead to substantially improved corrosion resistance due to the formation of a protective oxide layer. These studies show that engineering the surface/interface—by either adjusting its chemistry or structure—can meaningfully reduce corrosive attack, although the challenge of maintaining a robust, adherent barrier in extremely aggressive settings (such as molten aluminum) is not yet fully solved.
decision.unsolved: For boride-based components in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, the key unresolved issue is how to create a single, scalable intervention that yields a surface barrier stable at 600–750°C in contact with molten aluminum. In particular, it remains unclear how to prevent interdiffusion and chemical attack at the boride–aluminum interface with a minimal, single-step treatment.
decision.lever: Deposition of an ultrathin, dense alumina (Al2O3) layer via atomic layer deposition (ALD)
decision.why: Based on the trend that controlled surface modifications can drastically improve corrosion resistance by forming stable protective layers, the most plausible next step is to deposit an ALD-derived alumina film on the existing boride coating. Alumina is thermodynamically stable against molten aluminum, exhibits low diffusivity for aluminum atoms, and forms a chemically inert barrier. This single-step surface engineering intervention should improve corrosion resistance relative to standard boride coatings, as verified by weight-loss and microstructural analyses under 700°C molten aluminum exposure.
